customer_document_boundary: Customer-specific policy dates, prior continuous coverage, selected options, endorsements, declarations, and relevant medical history must be verified from the applicable customer documents before applying the rule to that customer.
definition: A Pre-Existing Disease (PED) means any condition, ailment, injury or disease that was diagnosed by a physician not more than 36 months before the policy commencement date, or for which medical advice or treatment was recommended or received from a physician not more than 36 months before policy commencement.

examples.scenario: A person already has an ear condition that was diagnosed 18 months before the health policy starts.
examples.result: That diagnosis falls within the 36-month look-back, so the condition fits the diagnosis-timing part of the PED definition.
examples.boundary: This example only explains what counts as a PED. It does not decide the product's PED waiting period, whether continuity or portability changes that period, or claim approval or payment.

limitations: This record explains the generic PED definition only.
It does not state any insurer-specific or product-specific PED waiting period.
It does not determine customer-specific PED status without the relevant dates and medical history.
It does not determine claim admissibility, approval, payment, entitlement, or recommendation.
plain_language_explanation: A Pre-Existing Disease (PED) is a health problem or medical condition you already had before your insurance started. Under the formal definition used here, the relevant look-back is 36 months for diagnosis, medical advice or treatment.
practical_implication: If a condition is a PED, the specific health plan may apply a PED waiting period before the PED waiting-period restriction ends. The actual waiting period, any continuity or portability credit, and any claim outcome must come from the applicable product terms and customer documents.
product_specific_boundary: The applicable PED waiting-period duration, optional modifications, continuity or portability credit, exclusions, and other product mechanics must come from governed product knowledge.
